rationale: Start with a broad gradient to locate the elution window and critical pairs while minimizing the risk of missing strongly retained compounds. A midrange temperature leaves room to probe temperature-dependent selectivity in either direction.

Lengthen only the gradient to test whether the two critical pairs respond to reduced slope. The last peak should remain near or below 10 minutes, allowing improved separation without a substantial time penalty.

The critical pair improved strongly with a shallower gradient. Raising phi0 narrows the gradient window and reduces its slope while advancing the last peak, aiming for full resolution below 10 minutes; the early peaks have ample separation to accommodate some compression.

Reduce the slope further while retaining the improved starting composition. The earlier slope test suggests this may bring the remaining critical pair to R ≥ 1.5, with the last peak still below 10 minutes.

Injection 4 reached the maximum CRF, so retain it as the benchmark. Increase temperature by one step to seek a shorter fully resolved separation and measure the critical pair’s temperature sensitivity.

The critical pair is strongly temperature-sensitive, and heating reduced its resolution. Test a cooler, shorter gradient to gain selectivity while offsetting the retention increase with a steeper slope.

Test whether stronger heating carries the temperature-sensitive pair through an elution-order reversal and restores separation. The shorter gradient also targets a substantially faster run; injection 4 remains the maximum-score fallback.
Test an intermediate temperature to avoid the new close pair seen at 60 C while seeking separation after the earlier pair’s order reversal. A 10-minute gradient targets a faster maximum-score method.

Return to the fully resolved 40 C condition and raise the starting organic fraction to advance the last peak while making the gradient shallower. Check whether the early peaks retain enough separation and the critical middle pair remains resolved.

At 50 C the original critical pair appears to have reversed order, so a steeper gradient may now improve its separation. Shorten only tG to test that response while monitoring the neighboring pair that had R = 1.74.

Test whether the steeper gradient separates the close pair seen at 60 C by moving it farther past its apparent order reversal. This also directly measures the temperature response relative to injection 10 while targeting a last peak near 5 minutes.

At 50 C one pair remains weakly separated, while 60 C creates a different close pair. Test 55 C with a shallower gradient to seek a selectivity balance that fully resolves both and elutes faster than injection 4.
The 55 C method is nearly fully resolved, with only one pair slightly below threshold. Lengthen the gradient one step to improve that pair while keeping the last peak below 10 minutes.

Raise the starting organic fraction one step from the fully resolved 55 C method to shorten retention while narrowing the gradient window. Check that both critical middle pairs and the early pair retain baseline resolution.

The latest run shows that higher starting organic strongly compresses the critical pair near the fourth peak. Lower phi0 to improve that selectivity while shortening tG to target full resolution faster than injection 13.
Injection 15 is the fastest fully resolved method so far. Shorten only tG by one grid step to test whether both critical pairs remain above R = 1.5 with a last peak near 7.2 minutes.

Reduce phi1 to obtain a slope between injections 15 and 16, aiming to recover full resolution with a last peak slightly earlier than injection 15. The last peak’s estimated elution composition is around 0.57, so 0.85 still provides ample final solvent strength.

Use a slightly steeper slope than injection 17 to trim retention while targeting R just above 1.5 for both critical pairs. The final organic fraction remains comfortably above the estimated last-peak elution composition.

Test whether a lower starting organic fraction improves the limiting pair enough to permit a steeper, faster gradient. Injection 18 remains the fastest confirmed maximum-score method; monitor the other critical pair for loss of selectivity.

Slightly reduce the slope from injection 19 to recover resolution of the limiting pair, while checking the second pair’s small margin above 1.5. This should elute the last peak sooner than injection 18 if full resolution is retained.

The 55 C region now has a well-defined resolution limit, with injection 20 retained as the fastest maximum-score method. Test the low-temperature endpoint for further elution-order changes that could open a different, faster fully resolved separation.

Return to the successful 55 C region and test a slope just steeper than injection 18. This probes whether its small resolution margin can support an earlier last peak while preserving the maximum CRF.

Trim injection 20’s unused high-organic tail while preserving its successful gradient slope. The last peak should still elute within the gradient, retaining maximum CRF with a shorter programmed gradient.

Test a compact gradient with the same successful slope and starting composition as injection 17, ending just above the estimated last-peak elution composition. This offers an alternative eight-minute program with slightly more resolution margin than injection 23.

Preserve injection 23’s successful slope through all closely spaced peaks, then test an earlier transition to the final hold. The isolated last peak may elute later but should remain below 10 minutes; injection 23 remains the fastest confirmed maximum-score fallback.
